sentences.text: Ekrixinatosaurus novasi is the sole species within the genus of abelisaurid theropods that roamed during the Early Cretaceous.
Its head was square and deeper than usual for a large carnivore, with jaws that curved upward.
The animal featured a large skull, a prominent brow ridge, and sturdy, shortened hind legs designed to withstand combat damage.
Teeth in the short upper jaw were flattened on the sides and bore serrations along both edges.
While early guesses placed its length between six and eight meters, a later study refined this to about 7.40 meters.
This revised size makes it slightly smaller than the related Carnotaurus, which measured 7.80 meters.
Argentine paleontologist Jorge Calvo and his Chilean colleagues David Rubilar-Rogers and Karen Moreno first named the creature in 2004.
The name Ekrixinatosaurus translates to 'lizard born from an explosion,' referencing the mining blast that uncovered the fossils.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as MUCPv-294, was a scattered skeleton containing parts of the skull, spine, pelvis, and leg bones.
This predator lived in the red sedimentary layers of the Candeleros Formation, a landscape teeming with diverse vertebrate life.
It shared its home range with massive sauropods like Andesaurus, Limaysaurus, and Nopcsaspondylus.
Evidence suggests the giant carnosaur Giganotosaurus may have been the dominant hunter in this same ecosystem.
The area also hosted smaller hunters such as the dromaeosaurid Buitreraptor, the alvarezsaurid Alnashetri, and the basal ceratosaurian Bicentenaria.
Taxonomists place this dinosaur within the family Abelisauridae.
Preliminary phylogenetic studies group it with Majungatholus and Carnotaurini as a sister taxon to Ilokelesia.
Fossils date to the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, specifically around 111.4 million years ago.
The fossil record indicates a time range spanning from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.

Scientists debate whether abelisaurids only became top predators after carcharodontosaurids went extinct, noting that the coexistence of large Giganotosaurus and Ekrixinatosaurus challenges this view.

However, the fact that both Giganotosaurus and Ekrixinatosaurus were among the largest in their respective groups while living together refutes the idea that abelisauroids only gained dominance after carnosaur extinction.
It remains uncertain whether these large predators occupied different ecological niches, such as active hunting versus scavenging.
